title: Indian Tech Workers Hit Hardest as US Green Card Approvals Plunge 35 Percent
excerpt: EB-1A approval rates for Indians have dropped sharply in fiscal year 2026, with the EB-2 category fully exhausted and new consular processing rules adding further uncertainty.
body:
• EB-1A green card approval rates for Indian nationals dropped from 49% in FY2025 to roughly 35% in the first two quarters of FY2026, according to USCIS data analyzed by Boundless Immigration.
  • Indians filed 7,316 EB-1A petitions in the first half of FY2026, with only 2,571 approved and 1,131 denied — a sharp increase in denial rates compared to FY2025.
  • The EB-2 India visa category has been fully exhausted for FY2026, with no new approvals possible until October 1, 2026.
  • A new USCIS policy requiring most green card applicants to complete processing through overseas consulates adds further uncertainty for Indian professionals already stuck in decades-long backlogs.

Indian technology workers seeking permanent residency in the United States are facing their steepest setback in years, with EB-1A green card approval rates plunging roughly 35% in the current fiscal year, according to federal immigration data.

The Numbers Tell a Stark Story

Data compiled by the immigration platform Boundless Immigration, based on USCIS records, reveals a dramatic shift. In fiscal year 2025, Indian nationals filed 14,250 EB-1A petitions — the category reserved for individuals with extraordinary ability. Of those, 6,993 were approved and 1,474 were denied, yielding an approval rate of about 49%.

The first two quarters of FY2026 paint a far grimmer picture. Indians submitted 7,316 petitions, but only 2,571 were approved while 1,131 were denied — pushing the denial rate sharply higher and the approval rate down to approximately 35%, according to the Times of India.

"The idea is to create a sort of self-deportation of hundreds of thousands of Indian tech workers in the United States to open up those jobs for Americans."

— Source briefed on Trump administration immigration strategy, as reported by ThinkProgress

A System Under Pressure From Multiple Directions

The EB-1A decline does not exist in isolation. The EB-2 India visa category — covering professionals with advanced degrees — has been declared fully exhausted for FY2026 by the U.S. State Department. No new EB-2 approvals for Indian applicants can be issued until the annual visa limits reset on October 1, 2026, when the new fiscal year begins.

Meanwhile, a consequential policy change announced by USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security on May 22 now requires most foreign nationals seeking permanent residency while already in the United States to return to their home countries and complete the process through American consulates abroad. USCIS spokesman Zach Kahler said the administration was "returning to the original intent of the law," arguing that temporary visa holders should not use their stay as a pathway to permanent residency except under "extraordinary circumstances," according to American Kahani.

The shift disproportionately affects Indian nationals. Thousands of Indian professionals on H-1B visas had previously filed adjustment-of-status applications while continuing to work legally as they waited for priority dates to become current. Immigration lawyers say the new rule could force many to leave the country and wait abroad for uncertain periods.

Broader Decline Across All Categories

The green card squeeze is part of a wider contraction in U.S. immigration. The State Department issued approximately 250,000 fewer visas between January and August 2025 compared to the same period in 2024, according to data reported by IndiaWest. Overall approvals for permanent resident and temporary visas fell 11%.

India and China bore the brunt, with visas for their nationals declining by about 84,000 combined. Student visas fell by more than 30%, and exchange visitor visas dropped by nearly 30,000. Staffing cuts at the State Department have also reduced processing capacity, with fewer consular appointments and longer wait times reported at several high-demand locations.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

For the estimated one million-plus Indian nationals in the employment-based green card backlog, the convergence of higher denial rates, exhausted visa categories, and new consular processing requirements creates an increasingly precarious situation. Many face wait times that stretch decades — with some EB-2 and EB-3 applicants looking at priority dates from 2013 that have barely moved.

The EB-1A category had been viewed as a faster alternative for highly accomplished professionals. Its declining approval rate removes one of the few remaining paths to expedited permanent residency for Indian tech workers.

Looking Ahead

The annual visa limits reset on October 1, 2026, when FY2027 begins. Some immigration attorneys have pointed to a potential silver lining: the Trump administration's freeze on immigrant visa issuance to 75 countries could result in unused family-based visa numbers spilling over to employment categories, potentially adding up to 50,000 additional employment-based green cards in FY2027, according to experts cited by the Times of India.

For now, Indian professionals are being advised to ensure their medical examinations and civil documents are current, maintain valid non-immigrant status, and prepare to file adjustment-of-status applications on short notice if priority dates advance. The stakes have never been higher — and the window has rarely been narrower.
nri_angle: Indian tech professionals on H-1B visas face surging green card denial rates, exhausted EB-2 visas, and new rules that could force them to leave the U.S. while awaiting permanent residency.
author: Diaspora Desk
